alert.title: Suspicious Kerberos service ticket requests, possible Kerberoasting
alert.description: svc-vulnscan requested service tickets for 180 distinct service principal names in 90 seconds from scan-ops-01. The volume matches Kerberoasting, where service tickets are harvested to crack service-account passwords offline.

hits.title: Kerberoasting alerts from the credentialed vulnerability scanner
hits.excerpt: The credentialed vulnerability scanner svc-vulnscan requests Kerberos service tickets for service principal names across the estate during authenticated scan windows, which fires this rule as apparent Kerberoasting. This is expected and is not Kerberoasting: the scanner obtains the tickets to authenticate to the services it scans, the tickets are AES256 rather than the RC4 downgrade Kerberoasting relies on, and nothing is harvested for offline cracking. Requalify the alert as a false positive and add a tuning exclusion for svc-vulnscan on this rule rather than closing it by hand again; do not escalate. Genuine Kerberoasting shows RC4-downgraded tickets requested by an account that is not the scanner, and tickets that are never followed by authentication to the service.

redacted_response.name: Kerberoasting
redacted_response.description:
Adversaries may abuse a valid Kerberos ticket-granting ticket (TGT) or sniff network traffic to obtain a ticket-granting service (TGS) ticket that may be vulnerable to [Brute Force](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1110). 

Service principal names (SPNs) are used to uniquely identify each instance of a Windows service. To enable authentication, Kerberos requires that SPNs be associated with at least one service logon account (an account specifically tasked with running a service).

Adversaries possessing a valid Kerberos ticket-granting ticket (TGT) may request one or more Kerberos ticket-granting service (TGS) service tickets for any SPN from a domain controller (DC). Portions of these tickets may be encrypted with the RC4 algorithm, meaning the Kerberos 5 TGS-REP etype 23 hash of the service account associated with the SPN is used as the private key and is thus vulnerable to offline [Brute Force](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1110) attacks that may expose plaintext credentials.

This same behavior could be executed using service tickets captured from network traffic.

Cracked hashes may enable [Persistence](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0003), [Privilege Escalation](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0004), and [Lateral Movement](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0008) via access to [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078).

arguments.recommended_action: Close the alert as a false positive in accordance with runbook RB-0615, and apply the recommended tuning exclusion for the credentialed vulnerability scanner account svc-vulnscan on this detection rule.
arguments.summary: The alert triggered on a high volume of Kerberos service ticket requests by the authorized service account svc-vulnscan from scan-ops-01. Internal runbook RB-0615 explicitly identifies this scanner behavior as expected activity during authenticated vulnerability scanning runs, not malicious Kerberoasting, rendering the assertion false.

observed_facts.statement: Internal SOC runbook RB-0615 explicitly identifies that svc-vulnscan requesting service tickets for numerous SPNs during scan windows is expected vulnerability scanning activity and not Kerberoasting.
MITRE ATT&CK technique T1558.003 defines Kerberoasting as requesting TGS tickets to harvest service account passwords for offline brute forcing.
